abstract: Vector quantization, a problem rooted in Shannon’s source coding theory, aims to quantize high-dimensional Euclidean vectors while minimizing distortion in their geometric structure. We propose TurboQuant to address both mean-squared error (MSE) and inner product distortion, overcoming limitations of existing methods that fail to achieve optimal distortion rates. Our data-oblivious algorithms, suitable for online applications, achieve near-optimal distortion rates (within a small constant factor) across all bit-widths and dimensions. TurboQuant achieves this by randomly rotating input vectors, inducing a concentrated Beta distribution on coordinates, and leveraging the near-independence property of distinct coordinates in high dimensions to simply apply optimal scalar quantizers per each coordinate. Recognizing that MSE-optimal quantizers introduce bias in inner product estimation, we propose a two-stage approach: applying an MSE quantizer followed by a 1-bit Quantized JL (QJL) transform on the residual, resulting in an unbiased inner product quantizer. We also provide a formal proof of the information-theoretic lower bounds on best achievable distortion rate by any vector quantizer, demonstrating that TurboQuant closely matches these bounds, differing only by a small constant ($\approx 2.7$) factor. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings, showing that for KV cache quantization, we achieve absolute quality neutrality with 3.5 bits per channel and marginal quality degradation with 2.5 bits per channel. Furthermore, in nearest neighbor search tasks, our method outperforms existing product quantization techniques in recall while reducing indexing time to virtually zero.

sections.body:
The section motivates vector quantization for KV cache compression and nearest neighbor search. It states that existing methods either lack accelerator compatibility or have suboptimal distortion bounds relative to bit-width.

TurboQuant is a two-stage method. The first stage randomly rotates each input vector, so each coordinate follows a Beta distribution, and applies a Lloyd-Max scalar quantizer to each coordinate to minimize mean-squared error. The second stage applies the 1-bit Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transform to the residual, which makes the inner product estimate unbiased.

The authors state that MSE-optimal quantizers alone give biased inner product estimates. They claim provably optimal distortion bounds for both MSE and inner products, with an exponential improvement in bit-width dependence.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: TurboQuant combines an MSE-optimal rotation-based quantizer with a 1-bit QJL residual stage to get unbiased, near-optimal inner product quantization.

sections.body:
This section gives the tools used in the proofs.

- Lemma 1 states that a coordinate of a uniform point on the unit hypersphere follows a scaled Beta distribution, which converges to a normal distribution with variance 1/d in high dimensions.
- Lemma 2 states the Shannon Lower Bound on MSE for a source with finite differential entropy.
- Lemma 3 specializes this to uniform points on the sphere, giving a bound of 2^(-2B/d).
- The QJL map takes the sign of a Gaussian matrix times x. Its dequantization is scaled by sqrt(pi/2)/d.
- Lemma 4 states that this estimator is unbiased, with variance at most pi/(2d) times the squared norm of y.

The section reports no empirical results.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Coordinates of a uniform hypersphere point follow a Beta law that tends to a normal law, and QJL gives an unbiased single-bit estimator.

sections.body:
This section gives the MSE-optimal TurboQuant method and a lower-bound proof. Each input on the unit sphere is multiplied by a random rotation built from the QR decomposition of a Gaussian matrix. Each coordinate then gets an optimal scalar quantizer, found by solving a one-dimensional k-means problem.

The printed centroids are ±sqrt(2/pi)/sqrt(d) at 1 bit and ±0.453/sqrt(d), ±1.51/sqrt(d) at 2 bits. The proof shows that the MSE equals d times the optimal k-means cost, which is bounded numerically for b=1 to 4.

The lower bound uses Shannon's lower bound and Yao's minimax principle. It states that any randomized quantizer has MSE at least 1/4^b on some input on the sphere. The authors note that coordinate independence holds only approximately in high dimensions.
sections.heading: TurboQuant: High Performance Quantization
sections.headline: MSE distortion is bounded by a constant times 1/4^b, reaching 0.36 at 1 bit and 0.009 at 4 bits.

sections.body:
Experiments run on a single accelerator. On 100,000 DBpedia Entities training vectors of dimension 1536, with 1,000 queries, TurboQuant mse shows inner product bias that grows with the average inner product at 2 bits. TurboQuant prod stays unbiased at every bit-width.

On needle-in-a-haystack with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over 4k to 104k tokens, TurboQuant reaches the full-precision score at more than 4× compression. The baselines are tested at a memory compression ratio of 0.25.

On LongBench-E, the 2.5-bit setting averages 49.44 against 50.06 for the full cache with Llama. For 4-bit nearest neighbor quantization, TurboQuant takes 0.0007 to 0.0021 seconds across dimensions 200 to 3072. Product quantization (PQ) takes 37.04 to 494.42 seconds. The authors note that PQ benefits from training and querying on the same data.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: TurboQuant matches full-precision performance on needle-in-a-haystack, and outperforms product quantization in recall while reducing indexing time to essentially zero.
